questions.title: Updating a Belief About a Strategy's Win Rate
questions.prompt: You're tracking a new signal and want to update your belief about its true win rate as trades come in, rather than just computing a raw hit rate. Explain how you'd use Bayesian inference with a Beta-Binomial model to do this, and why the posterior differs from the raw win rate after only a handful of trades.
questions.modelAnswer: Start with a prior belief about the win rate p, expressed as p ~ Beta(alpha, beta) -- a Beta(1,1) prior is uniform, representing 'no strong opinion yet.' After observing k wins out of n trades, the Binomial likelihood combines with the Beta prior to give a posterior that is again Beta: p | data ~ Beta(alpha + k, beta + (n - k)). This conjugacy means the update is pure algebra -- add wins to alpha, add losses to beta -- with no numerical integration required. The posterior mean, (alpha+k)/(alpha+beta+n), is a blend of the prior and the raw win rate k/n, and after only a few trades the prior still carries real weight, pulling the posterior mean toward the prior's center. That's exactly why a 70% win rate after 10 trades produces a posterior mean noticeably below 70% with a Beta(1,1) prior -- the data hasn't yet overwhelmed the prior's influence. As n grows, the k/n term dominates and the posterior converges to the raw win rate, exactly as you'd want.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I'd actually set this up: put a Beta(1,1) prior on the win rate if I genuinely have no strong view, then every time a trade closes, just update alpha with wins and beta with losses -- that's the entire update, no numerical work needed, which is the whole point of using a conjugate prior. The thing I'd specifically call out, because it's the part people get wrong, is that after only 10 trades with 7 wins, the posterior mean won't be exactly 0.70 -- it'll be pulled a bit toward 0.5 because the prior still has real weight relative to only 10 data points. That's a feature, not a bug: it's exactly the kind of overconfidence correction you want when someone shows you a 70% win rate from a tiny sample and wants to size a position based on it.
questions.example: Starting from Beta(1,1) and observing 7 wins out of 10 trades gives a posterior of Beta(8,4), with posterior mean 8/12 ≈ 0.667 -- noticeably below the raw 70% win rate, and you can also report a 95% credible interval directly from that posterior.
commonMistakes: Reporting the raw win rate k/n as if it were already the best estimate, ignoring how little data backs it
Confusing a Bayesian credible interval ('there's a 95% probability the true rate is in this range') with a frequentist confidence interval, which has a different meaning
Picking a Beta(1,1) prior and forgetting it still meaningfully shrinks the estimate toward 0.5 for small samples
Not updating the posterior incrementally as new trades arrive, and instead recomputing from scratch with ad hoc weighting
keyPoints: Beta prior + Binomial likelihood gives a Beta posterior: Beta(alpha+k, beta+n-k)
The update is pure algebra: add wins to alpha, losses to beta
Posterior mean is a blend of prior and raw win rate, more prior-weighted with small samples
As n grows, the posterior converges to the raw win rate
Credible intervals have a different meaning from frequentist confidence intervals

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly states the Beta-Binomial conjugate update
Explains why the posterior differs from the raw win rate with small samples
Mentions credible intervals and how they differ from confidence intervals
Clarity

questions.title: PCA as a Statistical Factor Model
questions.prompt: You run PCA on a panel of 200 equity return series and look at `explained_variance_ratio_`. Explain what the first principal component typically represents, and why that's not an accident of the math.
questions.modelAnswer: PCA finds the eigenvectors of the (standardized) return covariance matrix, ranked by the variance they explain -- the eigenvectors are orthogonal directions in return space, and each eigenvalue is exactly the variance of the portfolio defined by that eigenvector. Applied to a broad equity panel, the first principal component almost always loads positively on nearly every asset, because nearly every stock moves with the broad market to some degree; PCA finds that shared co-movement as the single direction that explains the most variance, without ever being told what 'the market' is. For a broad equity universe it's typical for PC1 alone to explain 30-50%+ of total variance, with a sharp drop-off after that. This isn't an artifact of the decomposition -- it's a structural fact about equity markets (systematic, market-wide co-movement dominates idiosyncratic movement), and it's exactly why PCA is used as a data-driven, assumption-light alternative to classical factor models like the Fama-French or APT framework: it recovers a 'market factor' and secondary factors directly from the covariance structure of the data.
questions.professionalAnswer: Whenever I run PCA on a wide equity panel and look at the explained-variance ratios, I expect the first component to come out looking like a market factor, and if it doesn't, that's actually the surprising result worth investigating. The reason is structural, not mathematical sleight of hand: most stocks have some positive co-movement with the broad market, so the direction that explains the most variance in the data is going to load broadly and positively across nearly everything -- PCA finds that because it's genuinely the dominant source of shared variance, not because PCA was told to look for 'the market.' In practice I've seen PC1 explain anywhere from 30% to over 50% of total variance on a diversified equity universe, with a steep drop to PC2. The later components are harder to interpret cleanly, but they often loosely track known style factors like size or sector groupings.
commonMistakes: Assuming PCA 'knows' what the market factor is, rather than it emerging purely from the variance structure
Forgetting to standardize returns before PCA, letting a few high-volatility names dominate the components
Treating later principal components as equally interpretable as the first one
Not distinguishing PCA's uncorrelated components from a classical factor model's economically-motivated factors
keyPoints: PCA finds orthogonal variance-maximizing directions via the covariance matrix's eigendecomposition
Each eigenvalue equals the variance explained by its corresponding component
PC1 in a broad equity panel typically loads broadly and positively -- the informal 'market factor'
This reflects real market structure, not an artifact of the math
Standardizing returns before PCA matters, since PCA is scale-sensitive

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains PCA's relationship to the covariance matrix's eigendecomposition
Explains why PC1 typically resembles a market factor
Mentions standardization and typical explained-variance magnitudes

questions.title: GARCH(1,1) and the Persistence of Volatility
questions.prompt: Explain what a GARCH(1,1) model is capturing that a simple historical (rolling-window) volatility estimate misses, and what the stationarity condition alpha + beta < 1 actually means in practice.
questions.modelAnswer: A rolling-window historical volatility estimate just averages squared returns over a fixed window, treating every day in that window equally and giving no model of how volatility evolves. GARCH(1,1) instead models the conditional variance explicitly as sigma_t^2 = omega + alpha*eps_(t-1)^2 + beta*sigma_(t-1)^2, where alpha captures how strongly a fresh shock moves today's variance and beta captures how much of yesterday's variance persists into today. This lets the model react immediately to a large shock (through alpha) while also remembering that volatility was already elevated (through beta) -- producing the volatility clustering seen in real markets, where a turbulent period tends to stay turbulent for a while rather than snapping back to normal immediately. The condition alpha + beta < 1 is what guarantees the process has a well-defined, finite long-run average variance (the model is covariance stationary); if alpha + beta were close to or above 1, shocks to volatility would decay very slowly or not at all, meaning any given shock has a near-permanent effect on the variance forecast -- in practice, real equity data often shows beta in the 0.85-0.95 range, meaning volatility shocks decay slowly and a turbulent week can leave the market jumpy for a long stretch afterward.
questions.professionalAnswer: A rolling-window vol estimate is really just a blunt average -- every day in the window counts the same, and it has no sense of 'volatility is itself evolving.' GARCH(1,1) actually models that evolution: alpha tells you how much a fresh shock moves today's variance forecast, and beta tells you how much of yesterday's elevated variance is still hanging around today. That combination is what produces volatility clustering -- a big move today raises tomorrow's forecast immediately, and if beta is high, that elevated level persists for a while rather than reverting instantly. The alpha+beta<1 condition is the thing I always check first when I fit one of these -- it's what guarantees the model has a sensible long-run variance to revert to. In real equity data I almost always see beta sitting somewhere around 0.85 to 0.95, which tells you volatility shocks are quite persistent -- a bad week leaves the market jumpy for a good while afterward, not just the next day.
questions.example: arch_model(returns, vol='Garch', p=1, q=1).fit() in Python's `arch` package returns omega, alpha[1], and beta[1] directly, and res.forecast(horizon=10) projects the conditional variance forward using exactly this recursive formula.
commonMistakes: Describing GARCH as just 'a fancier moving average' without mentioning it models conditional variance as its own recursive process
Confusing the ARCH (q) and GARCH (p) lag conventions, which are the opposite of ARIMA's (p,d,q) convention
Not checking alpha + beta < 1 before trusting a fitted model's long-run variance forecast
Assuming GARCH automatically captures the leverage effect (asymmetric response to negative shocks), which plain GARCH(1,1) does not
keyPoints: GARCH(1,1): sigma_t^2 = omega + alpha*eps_(t-1)^2 + beta*sigma_(t-1)^2
alpha measures reaction to a fresh shock; beta measures persistence of past variance
This produces volatility clustering, which a static rolling-window estimate cannot represent
alpha + beta < 1 is required for a finite, well-defined long-run variance (stationarity)
Real equity data often shows high beta (0.85-0.95), implying slow-decaying volatility shocks

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly states the GARCH(1,1) recursion and the roles of alpha and beta
Explains what GARCH captures that rolling-window volatility misses
Correctly explains the alpha+beta<1 stationarity condition

questions.title: Why Ordinary K-Fold Cross-Validation Leaks on Time Series
questions.prompt: A colleague wants to use scikit-learn's standard `KFold` (with `shuffle=False`) to validate a return-prediction model on daily data. Explain why this still leaks future information into training, and how `TimeSeriesSplit` fixes it. Then explain what `TimeSeriesSplit` alone still does NOT fix.
questions.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold, TimeSeriesSplit

# BAD for time series:
kf = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=False)

# Enforces train strictly before test in time:
tscv = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5)
questions.modelAnswer: Even with `shuffle=False`, plain `KFold` rotates which fold is held out as the test set, so for every fold except the very first, the training set contains rows that come from *after* the test period in calendar time -- the model is trained partly on the future and evaluated on the past, making it look better than it has any right to. `TimeSeriesSplit` fixes this directly: given data sorted by time, every test fold comes strictly after its corresponding training fold, by default using an expanding window (training grows each split) or, if `max_train_size` is set, a rolling window of fixed size. What `TimeSeriesSplit` does NOT fix is leakage from overlapping label windows: if a label is 'the return over the next 5 days,' a training observation sitting just before the test boundary can have a label that reaches into the test period even though its own timestamp is safely before it. Time order alone guarantees train precedes test in timestamp, but not that a training label's underlying window stays entirely out of the test span -- that's exactly the gap that purging and embargoing close.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I'd point out first is that `shuffle=False` doesn't save plain `KFold` here -- the leak isn't from randomization, it's from fold rotation. Every fold gets a turn as the test set, so except for the very first one, your training data for that fold includes rows from after the test period. `TimeSeriesSplit` fixes exactly that: train is always strictly before test, period, whether you use its default expanding window or cap it with `max_train_size` for a rolling window instead. But I'd immediately flag the thing that trips people up next: `TimeSeriesSplit` only guarantees order on the raw timestamp. If your label is a forward-looking return -- 'what happens over the next 5 days' -- a training row sitting right before the test boundary can have a label that's computed using data from inside the test window. `TimeSeriesSplit` has no idea that's happening; it only looks at row position, not at what the label itself depends on. That's a different, additional leak that needs purging to fix.
commonMistakes: Assuming `shuffle=False` alone makes ordinary KFold safe for time series
Believing TimeSeriesSplit's time-ordering guarantee is sufficient for any kind of label
Not knowing TimeSeriesSplit supports both expanding and rolling (max_train_size) windows
Forgetting that the `gap` parameter in TimeSeriesSplit exists but still isn't the same as proper purging for overlapping labels
keyPoints: Plain KFold leaks future-into-past because every fold rotates into the test role, with or without shuffling
TimeSeriesSplit guarantees train always precedes test in calendar time
Expanding window (default) keeps all history; rolling window (max_train_size) caps training set size
TimeSeriesSplit does not account for forward-looking label windows overlapping the test set
That remaining gap is what purging and embargoing are built to close

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why plain KFold leaks even without shuffling
Correctly explains how TimeSeriesSplit fixes ordering
Correctly identifies what TimeSeriesSplit does NOT fix (overlapping label windows)
Code correctness

questions.title: Deriving the MLE for an Exponential Distribution
questions.prompt: Derive the maximum likelihood estimator for the rate parameter lambda of an Exponential(lambda) distribution, given n i.i.d. observations x_1, ..., x_n. Then write the one line of Python that computes it from a NumPy array of observations.
questions.modelAnswer: The density is f(x; lambda) = lambda * e^(-lambda*x), so the log-likelihood is ell(lambda) = n*log(lambda) - lambda*sum(x_i). Differentiating and setting to zero: ell'(lambda) = n/lambda - sum(x_i) = 0, which gives lambda_hat_MLE = n / sum(x_i) = 1/x_bar -- the reciprocal of the sample mean. This matches the known fact that E[X] = 1/lambda for the exponential distribution, so setting the sample mean equal to the theoretical mean (which is also what Method of Moments would give here) recovers the same estimator. In NumPy: `lam_mle = 1 / x.mean()`.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd just do the calculus directly: log-likelihood is n*log(lambda) minus lambda times the sum of the observations, take the derivative with respect to lambda, set it to zero, and solve -- you get lambda_hat equals n over the sum of x_i, which is just one over the sample mean. It's a nice derivation because it also matches Method of Moments here, since E[X] = 1/lambda for an exponential, so matching the sample mean to the theoretical mean gives you the exact same formula -- that agreement is a good sanity check that the derivation is right. In code it's just `1 / x.mean()`, and I'd usually cross-check it against `scipy.stats.expon.fit(x, floc=0)` to make sure the closed form and the general-purpose numerical fit agree.
questions.example: rng.exponential(scale=1/250, size=2000) simulated data recovers lam_mle = 1/returns.mean() that matches scipy's expon.fit() closed form almost exactly.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to take the log of the likelihood before differentiating, making the algebra much messier
Mixing up the exponential's 'rate' parameterization (lambda) with its 'scale' parameterization (1/lambda), which is what scipy and NumPy actually use by default
Not checking the second derivative (or just reasoning about the shape) to confirm it's a maximum, not a minimum
Writing the estimator as lambda_hat = x_bar instead of 1/x_bar
keyPoints: Log-likelihood: n*log(lambda) - lambda*sum(x_i)
Setting the derivative to zero gives lambda_hat_MLE = n / sum(x_i) = 1/x_bar
This matches the Method of Moments estimator for this particular distribution
NumPy: `1 / x.mean()`

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct derivation of the log-likelihood and its derivative
Correct final estimator (1/x_bar)
Correct one-line NumPy code
Clarity

questions.title: Rolling Z-Score vs. Global Z-Score
questions.prompt: You're normalizing a rolling-sum trading-volume feature before feeding it into a model. Write the code for a rolling z-score transform, and explain why using a single global z-score (computed once over the whole dataset) is a leakage bug rather than just a different modeling choice.
questions.code:
def rolling_zscore(series, window=60):
    roll_mean = series.rolling(window).mean()
    roll_std = series.rolling(window).std()
    return (series - roll_mean) / roll_std
questions.modelAnswer: A rolling z-score re-centers and re-scales a feature using only a trailing window of recent history, `(x_t - rolling_mean_t) / rolling_std_t`, which adapts to a drifting mean or a changing volatility regime. A global z-score instead subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation computed once over the entire dataset, including rows that are chronologically in the future relative to any earlier point in the sample. That's a leakage bug, not a neutral modeling choice, because at any historical point t, the global mean and standard deviation used to normalize x_t were partly computed from data that didn't exist yet at time t -- the feature at time t secretly 'knows' something about the future distribution of the series. It's also a statistically weaker choice even ignoring leakage, since a global z-score assumes the feature's distribution is stable across the whole sample, which fails across a genuine regime change. Confirming the fix typically means running the ADF test before and after: a trending or regime-shifting raw feature fails to reject the unit-root null, while the same feature after a rolling z-score usually rejects it decisively.
questions.professionalAnswer: The code itself is simple -- rolling mean, rolling std, subtract and divide, all using `.rolling(window)` so nothing outside the trailing window is touched. The part I'd really want to get across in an interview is why a global z-score is a bug and not just 'a simpler way to normalize.' If I compute the mean and std once over the entire history and use that single pair of numbers to normalize a value from five years ago, that value's normalized score depends on data that didn't exist yet at that point in time -- that's leakage, full stop, not a stylistic difference. On top of that, it's just a worse assumption statistically, because it assumes the feature's distribution never shifts across the whole sample, and in real market data that's rarely true. I always confirm this kind of fix worked by running an ADF test before and after -- if the rolling z-score version passes and the raw feature or the global z-score version doesn't, that's the fix actually working, not just code that runs without error.
questions.example: A global z-score of a raw price level has identical ADF statistics to the untransformed price level itself, because it's just a fixed linear rescaling -- it does nothing to remove a trend, which is a useful fact to check directly if someone claims a global z-score 'fixed' non-stationarity.
commonMistakes: Treating a global z-score as a harmless convenience rather than a leakage bug
Using `.rolling(window)` but forgetting the window must end strictly before the row it's attached to (an off-by-one leak)
Not re-running an ADF test after the transform to confirm stationarity was actually achieved
Assuming any normalization automatically fixes non-stationarity, when a fixed linear rescaling cannot remove a trend
keyPoints: Rolling z-score uses only a trailing window's mean/std, adapting to drift and regime change
A global z-score uses full-sample statistics, including future-relative-to-any-point data -- that's leakage
A global z-score also assumes a stable distribution across the whole sample, which often fails
The ADF test is the standard way to confirm a stationarity fix actually worked

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct rolling z-score implementation
Correctly explains why a global z-score is leakage, not just a weaker choice
Mentions regime-change / distributional stability as an additional problem
Clarity

questions.title: A Feature That Suddenly Stops Working
questions.prompt: A feature that drove a profitable signal for two years suddenly starts contributing nothing -- or actively hurting performance -- in live trading, even though nothing about the model's code changed. Walk through how you'd diagnose this.
questions.modelAnswer: The first hypothesis should be non-stationarity in the underlying relationship, not a code bug: financial relationships are not fixed, and a feature that worked well in one market regime can go flat or invert in another. The diagnostic is to stop looking at a single full-sample importance or correlation number and instead compute the feature's Information Coefficient (the rank correlation between its predicted values and actual forward returns) in rolling windows over time. If the IC series shows a clear decay toward zero, or a reversal in sign, in the recent period relative to earlier history, that confirms the feature's relationship with returns has genuinely changed rather than the model simply hitting bad luck. It's also worth checking whether the feature itself has become non-stationary in a new way -- for example if it's built from a rolling-sum or price-level quantity that has drifted into a different regime -- since that can independently degrade a previously well-behaved feature. Only after ruling out a genuine regime shift would a code or data-pipeline bug become the next most likely explanation.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first instinct here is not to assume the code broke -- it's to assume the relationship itself changed, because that's exactly what financial signals do. I'd pull up the feature's rolling Information Coefficient over time rather than looking at one aggregate number, and see whether it's been quietly decaying or flipping sign over the recent window versus the two good years. If the IC series shows a clear decay or reversal, that's the real story -- the signal's edge faded, which is a very different problem from 'something is broken' and calls for a different response, like reconsidering whether to keep trading it at all rather than debugging code that was never wrong. I'd also double check the feature's own stationarity, since a rolling-sum or price-level-derived feature can drift into a new regime on its own and degrade a previously fine signal independent of anything about the target. Only after that would I go check the data pipeline for something more mundane, like a vendor change or a timezone shift.
commonMistakes: Jumping straight to debugging code before checking whether the signal's underlying relationship has simply changed
Relying on a single full-sample importance or correlation metric instead of a rolling diagnostic
Not distinguishing a genuine regime shift from a one-off bad stretch that could just be noise
Forgetting that the feature itself, not just its relationship to the target, can become non-stationary over time
keyPoints: Non-stationarity of the underlying relationship is the primary hypothesis, not a code bug
Compute a rolling Information Coefficient to see whether the signal's predictive power has decayed or reversed
Check whether the feature itself has drifted into a new statistical regime
Only investigate pipeline/data bugs after ruling out a genuine regime shift

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies non-stationarity/regime change as the leading hypothesis
Proposes a rolling IC or rolling-importance diagnostic
Considers the feature's own stationarity as a separate angle
Clarity and logical ordering of the diagnostic process

questions.title: The Off-by-One Rolling Window Leak
questions.prompt: A teammate built a 5-day moving-average feature with `ret.rolling(5).mean()` to predict the same day's return, and it shows a suspiciously strong correlation with the target. What's wrong, and how do you fix it?
questions.code:
df["ma5"] = ret.rolling(5).mean()   # ends ON day t -- includes ret[t] itself!
correct_feature = df["ma5"].shift(1)  # fix: shift back one day
questions.modelAnswer: `ret.rolling(5).mean()` computed on day t includes ret[t] itself as one of the five values being averaged, which means the 'feature' being used to predict today's return already partially contains today's own return. This is the off-by-one rolling-window leak: the window, as written, ends ON the row it's attached to rather than ending strictly before it. The fix is a one-character change: `.shift(1)` on the resulting series, so the feature value attached to day t only uses information available through yesterday's close. The practical impact of this bug is large, not subtle -- in a documented worked example on synthetic noise data, the leaky feature showed R^2 around 0.20 against the target, while the honestly shifted version showed R^2 around 0.0001, correctly revealing there was no real signal there at all. Every rolling-window feature should be checked against one question: does this window end strictly before the row it's attached to?
questions.professionalAnswer: This is one of the most common bugs I see, and it's exactly as described: `rolling(5).mean()` on day t's row includes day t's own value in the average, so you've built a feature that's partially made of the thing you're trying to predict. The fix is trivially small in code -- just add `.shift(1)` -- but the effect of not catching it is huge. I've seen this exact pattern produce an R^2 around 0.20 on data that has zero real signal in it, and the honest, shifted version comes back at essentially 0.0001, which is the true number. My habit now is to treat any suspiciously strong rolling-feature correlation as guilty until proven innocent -- the first thing I check is literally 'does this window end strictly before the target row,' because that one question catches this bug every time.
questions.example: On a synthetic i.i.d. noise series, the leaky ma5 feature showed corr ≈ 0.45 (R^2 ≈ 0.20) against today's return, while the correctly shifted feature showed corr ≈ 0.01 (R^2 ≈ 0.0001) — the honest answer for data with no real autocorrelation.
commonMistakes: Not realizing a rolling window 'ending on' the current row includes the current row's own value
Celebrating a strong in-sample correlation instead of treating it as suspicious
Fixing this inconsistently across some features but not others in the same pipeline
Forgetting this same off-by-one issue applies to rolling standard deviations, sums, and other rolling-window features, not just means
keyPoints: rolling(5).mean() on day t includes ret[t] itself unless shifted
The feature circularly contains part of the thing it's predicting -- classic leakage
Fix: .shift(1) so the feature only uses information through yesterday's close
An inflated in-sample correlation/R^2 is a symptom, not something to celebrate
Every rolling-window feature should be checked: does it end strictly before its target row?

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the off-by-one rolling-window leak
Correctly proposes the .shift(1) fix
Explains why the inflated correlation is a red flag rather than good news
Clarity

questions.title: Designing a Research Data Layer
questions.prompt: You're setting up a research codebase from scratch for a small team of three researchers. Describe the design of a data-access layer that will keep their notebooks consistent as data sources evolve, including how you'd handle caching and schema consistency.
questions.modelAnswer: The core design principle is that research code should ask for data by meaning, not by file path: functions like `load_prices(universe, start, end)` or `load_fundamentals(ticker, as_of)` that hide whatever the underlying source actually is -- a CSV, a Parquet file, a REST API, a database table -- behind a stable interface. The function's output contract (column names, dtypes, what a row represents, timezone convention) stays fixed even if the source changes underneath it, which is the entire point: a vendor swap or a schema change in the raw data gets fixed once, inside the function, instead of touching every notebook that calls it. For caching, something as simple as `functools.lru_cache` is often enough for a single research session, since the cache key is just the function's arguments and it avoids redundant reads of the same universe/date-range combination; for caching that needs to survive across process restarts, a disk-backed cache is the natural next step. For schema consistency, the data layer should normalize every source to the same column names, dtypes, and timezone handling on the way in -- resolving, once, the fact that a vendor file might call the date column 'Date' and store it in US Eastern time while another source calls it 'trade_date' in naive UTC -- so downstream research code never has to special-case which source a row originally came from.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd design this around one idea: nobody writing research code should ever see a raw file path or a vendor's column names directly. I'd build small functions like `load_prices(universe, start, end)` that do the messy work once -- reading whatever the actual source is, renaming columns to a consistent contract, normalizing timezones -- and have every notebook on the team call those functions instead of reading files themselves. That buys two things immediately: when a vendor changes something, I fix it in one place, and three researchers can't accidentally get three slightly different answers from 'the same' data because one of them handled a timezone differently. For caching, I'd start with `functools.lru_cache` for in-session speed since it's basically free to add, and only reach for a disk-backed cache once it's clear the same expensive reads are happening across separate sessions often enough to matter. The schema piece is honestly the part that pays off the most and gets noticed the least -- getting column names, dtypes, and timezone handling consistent across every source, once, in the data layer, rather than three researchers each guessing at it slightly differently in their own notebooks.
commonMistakes: Designing the interface around how the data happens to be stored today instead of what the caller actually needs
Skipping schema normalization and letting each notebook handle column-name or timezone differences independently
Jumping straight to a heavyweight caching/versioning solution before a simple in-memory cache is even needed
Not planning for the interface's output contract to stay stable even as the underlying source changes
keyPoints: Design functions around meaning (load_prices(universe, start, end)), not file paths
The output contract (columns, dtypes, timezone) stays stable even if the source changes
functools.lru_cache is a reasonable first caching layer; disk-backed caching for cross-session needs
Normalize schema/timezone once in the data layer, not independently in every notebook
This prevents silent disagreement between researchers using 'the same' data

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a stable, meaning-based interface design
Addresses caching with a reasonable, appropriately-scoped solution
Addresses schema/timezone consistency across sources
Clarity and practical framing for a small team

questions.title: I Can't Reproduce Last Week's Backtest Result
questions.prompt: A researcher reruns a notebook from last week and gets a meaningfully different Sharpe ratio, even though they're confident they didn't change any code. How do you figure out what happened, and how would you prevent this going forward?
questions.modelAnswer: A backtest result depends on three things: the code, the parameters, and the data. If the researcher is confident the code didn't change, the most likely remaining culprit is the data -- a vendor restated some fundamentals, a corporate action got applied differently, or a data pull happened to land on a slightly different day's universe, none of which show up in a git diff of the code. The fix going forward is two linked habits: experiment tracking (logging, for every run, the parameters and the resulting metrics so every run is queryable later -- even a simple logged row per run gets most of the value, though a framework like MLflow formalizes it) and data versioning (recording a fingerprint of the exact data used, as simply as a SHA-256 hash of the dataset's bytes, alongside the run's logged parameters and metrics). With both in place, 'reproduce last week's result' becomes a lookup -- find the run with this exact data fingerprint and these exact parameters -- instead of archaeology through old notebook outputs.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move wouldn't be to re-read the code -- it would be to ask what changed about the data between then and now, because 'the code didn't change' almost never means 'nothing that could affect the result changed.' A vendor restating a few numbers, a corporate action getting applied differently, a data pull landing on a slightly different universe snapshot -- none of that shows up in git history, and it's the single most common cause of this exact complaint. Going forward, I'd want two things in place: log every run's parameters and resulting metrics somewhere queryable, even if it's just a CSV row with a timestamp to start, and compute a hash of the exact data used in each run and log that alongside it. Once both exist, 'why can't I reproduce last week's number' turns into 'let me look up the run with this exact data fingerprint and these exact parameters' instead of a week of guessing.

Relying on memory or chat history to reconstruct what inputs produced a past result
Treating experiment tracking and data versioning as separate concerns rather than two halves of the same reproducibility story
Jumping straight to a heavyweight tool (like full DVC) before even basic parameter/metric logging and file hashing are in place

Together, these turn 'why can't I reproduce this' into a direct lookup rather than guesswork

questions.title: Communicating Uncertainty, Not Just a Point Estimate
questions.prompt: Your model estimates a strategy's true win rate as 58%, based on a Bayesian update from 40 trades. A portfolio manager asks you to just 'tell them the number' so they can size a position. How do you communicate the uncertainty behind that number without the conversation turning into a stats lecture?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer leads with the number the PM asked for, then immediately attaches a plain-language range rather than a lecture: something like '58% is our best estimate, but with only 40 trades behind it, the real number could reasonably be anywhere from about 45% to 70% -- that's a wide range, and it matters for how much confidence you put in the 58% specifically.' The key communication move is translating a credible interval into a decision-relevant statement ('don't size this as if 58% were exact') rather than explaining what a Beta posterior or a credible interval actually is. It's also worth proactively stating what would tighten that range -- more trades -- so the PM understands the uncertainty is a function of sample size, not a flaw in the model, and knows what to expect if they ask again after another 40 trades.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd give them the number first, because that's genuinely what they asked for and burying it doesn't help anyone -- '58%, that's our best estimate.' Then I'd immediately follow with the uncertainty in plain terms, not in Bayesian vocabulary: 'with only 40 trades, that 58% could realistically be anywhere from the mid-40s to around 70%, so I wouldn't size this as if 58% were a precise, locked-in number.' I think the mistake would be either hiding the uncertainty entirely, which sets them up to be surprised later, or going into a full explanation of credible intervals and posteriors, which is the stats lecture they explicitly didn't ask for. I'd close by telling them what actually narrows that range -- more trades -- so they know this isn't a permanent limitation, just where we are right now with the data we have.
commonMistakes: Either hiding the uncertainty entirely or over-explaining the statistical machinery behind it
Giving the range without translating it into what it means for position sizing
Not proactively stating what would reduce the uncertainty going forward
Treating the PM's request for 'just the number' as license to drop the uncertainty from the conversation

Translate statistical uncertainty into a decision-relevant statement about position sizing
Avoid jargon (credible interval, posterior) in favor of a concrete range
Explain what would narrow the uncertainty (more data), framing it as temporary, not permanent

questions.title: When a Result Doesn't Replicate
questions.prompt: You presented a promising signal to your team two weeks ago. A teammate just reran your analysis on a slightly extended data window and the effect has nearly vanished. How do you handle this conversation and the follow-up work?
questions.modelAnswer: The right first move is curiosity, not defensiveness: treat the non-replication as new information rather than an attack on the original work, and systematically rule out the mundane explanations before assuming the original finding was wrong. That means checking whether the extended window introduced a genuine regime change the original signal never saw, whether the teammate's rerun used the exact same data vintage and parameters, and whether the original result depended on a specific lucky stretch of history that a slightly longer window now dilutes. Once the cause is identified, the researcher should communicate it plainly to the team -- including the honest version if it turns out the original result doesn't hold up -- rather than quietly re-tuning parameters until the extended window 'works' again, which would just reintroduce the same overfitting problem the original research was supposed to avoid.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first reaction would genuinely be curiosity rather than defensiveness -- a result that doesn't replicate on more data is exactly the kind of thing good research culture is supposed to surface, and getting defensive about it would be the wrong instinct. I'd start by making sure it's an apples-to-apples comparison: same parameters, same data vintage, same preprocessing, before assuming anything about the original finding. If it turns out the extended window just happened to add a different market regime, or the original result was riding on a specific lucky stretch of history, I'd want to say that plainly to the team rather than quietly tweaking parameters until the number looks good again on the new window -- because that would just be re-introducing the exact overfitting problem the original validation was supposed to catch in the first place. I think how you handle this moment says more about your research judgment than the original result ever did.
commonMistakes: Getting defensive and looking for reasons to dismiss the teammate's rerun rather than investigating it
Re-tuning parameters on the extended window until the result looks good again, reintroducing overfitting
Not communicating the non-replication honestly to the rest of the team
Jumping to 'the original result was wrong' before ruling out mundane explanations like a data or parameter mismatch
keyPoints: Treat non-replication as information, not an attack -- respond with curiosity, not defensiveness
Rule out mundane causes first: parameter/data mismatches between the two runs
Consider whether a genuine regime change or a lucky original stretch explains the gap
Communicate the honest outcome to the team rather than quietly re-tuning until it 'works' again

questions.title: Framing a Research Question Before Touching the Data
questions.prompt: A PM tells you, 'go see if there's any interesting signal in our options-flow data.' Before you write any code, how do you turn that into an actual research question?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer resists the pull to immediately start exploring the data and instead pins down a specific, falsifiable hypothesis first: what exactly is being predicted (next-day return? a volatility event? direction over some horizon?), over what universe and time horizon, and what would count as a real, actionable effect versus a curiosity. Writing this down before looking at the data matters because it sets a pre-registered target, which makes it possible to later say honestly how many things were tried to find whatever result eventually turns up -- a vague, open-ended mandate like 'see if there's anything interesting' is exactly the setup that invites unconsciously trying dozens of framings until one looks good, which is a multiple-testing problem wearing the costume of open-minded exploration. The researcher should also clarify success criteria with the PM up front (what Sharpe, what sample size, what level of statistical significance would make this worth pursuing further) so the research has a stopping point instead of continuing indefinitely in search of a positive result.

I'd also want to agree on success criteria with the PM before I start, not after I find something that looks good, because otherwise it's very easy to unconsciously try framing after framing until one happens to look promising, which is a multiple-testing problem dressed up as open-minded exploration. Writing the actual hypothesis down first also means that whatever I find later, I can honestly say how many things I tried to get there, which is exactly the kind of transparency that makes a result trustworthy instead of just impressive-looking.

questions.title: Why Gradient Descent Moves Opposite the Gradient
questions.prompt: Explain why gradient descent updates parameters by moving in the direction of the negative gradient, not the gradient itself, and connect this to how an option trader interprets the Hessian of value with respect to price.
questions.modelAnswer: The gradient of f at a point, grad f(x), points in the direction of steepest increase of f at that point, with magnitude equal to the rate of increase in that direction. To minimize f -- reduce it fastest -- you move in the exact opposite direction, -grad f(x), the direction of steepest decrease. Each gradient-descent step, x_new = x - lr*grad f(x), is a direct application of this geometric fact, repeated until grad f(x) is approximately zero (a stationary point). The Hessian -- the matrix of second partial derivatives -- describes curvature at that point; for a scalar function like an option's value as a function of the underlying price, the Hessian is exactly gamma, the second derivative of value with respect to price, telling the trader how fast delta itself will change as price moves.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through the geometry directly: the gradient always points toward where the function increases fastest, so if you want to decrease the function, you flip the sign and walk the other way -- that's the entire justification for the minus sign in every gradient-descent update. You repeat that step, shrinking it with a learning rate, until the gradient is essentially zero, which is where you've stopped being able to improve locally. The Hessian connection is a nice one to make explicit: it's curvature, full stop, whether you're calling it 'the Hessian' in an optimizer's convergence analysis or 'gamma' on a trading desk -- both are the second derivative telling you how fast the first derivative itself is changing.
commonMistakes: Confusing the gradient's direction (steepest increase) with the direction you should move to minimize (its negative)
Forgetting the gradient's magnitude also matters -- it combines with the learning rate to set the step size
Not connecting the Hessian concept across domains -- it's curvature whether called 'the Hessian' in an optimizer or 'gamma' on a trading desk
keyPoints: Gradient points toward steepest increase
Moving along -grad f(x) decreases f fastest
Gradient descent repeats this step until grad f approx 0
Hessian = curvature = gamma in the option-pricing context

Correctly explains why descent moves along the negative gradient

questions.title: Why the Characteristic Function Exists When the MGF Doesn't
questions.prompt: A heavy-tailed return distribution has no moment-generating function in some neighborhood of zero, but it always has a characteristic function. Explain why, and why this matters for working with sums of independent heavy-tailed variables.
questions.modelAnswer: The MGF, M(t)=E[e^(tX)], requires the expectation of e^(tX) to be finite for t in some open interval around 0; for a sufficiently heavy-tailed distribution, e^(tX) grows faster than the tail decays, making that expectation infinite for any nonzero t, so the MGF simply doesn't exist there. The characteristic function, phi(t)=E[e^(itX)], replaces the real exponent with an imaginary one, and because |e^(itX)|=1 for every outcome, the expectation is always finite -- phi(t) exists and satisfies |phi(t)|<=1 for every distribution, heavy-tailed or not. This matters for sums of independent variables because phi_(X+Y)(t)=phi_X(t)*phi_Y(t) always holds, turning what would otherwise require an intractable convolution of densities into simple multiplication -- a tool that still works even when the MGF-based version of the same trick is unavailable.
questions.professionalAnswer: The key fact I'd lead with: the MGF needs E[e^(tX)] to be finite near zero, and for a heavy-tailed distribution that exponential can simply blow up faster than the tail decays, so the MGF doesn't exist at all. The characteristic function sidesteps this entirely by using an imaginary exponent -- |e^(itX)|=1 no matter what X is, so the expectation is bounded by 1 automatically, with zero finiteness condition needed. Why this actually matters in practice: the product rule for sums of independent variables, phi of the sum equals the product of the phis, still works perfectly with characteristic functions even when the MGF-based version of the same trick fails for a heavy-tailed series -- which is exactly the kind of series quant researchers deal with constantly.

Forgetting the key practical advantage of the characteristic function is that it always exists, with no finiteness condition
Not recognizing that the product rule for sums of independent variables is the real payoff, not an abstract curiosity

CF of a sum of independents is the product of CFs, same structure as MGF when it exists
This underlies both the CLT's proof and Fourier-based option pricing methods

questions.title: Why a Stock's Discounted Price, Not Its Raw Price, Is a Martingale
questions.prompt: Explain why a stock's raw real-world price process is generally NOT a martingale, but its discounted price under the risk-neutral measure is. What does this have to do with arbitrage?
questions.modelAnswer: A martingale requires E[X_t | F_s] = X_s -- the best forecast of a future value, given everything known now, is just the current value, with zero expected drift. A raw stock price under the real-world measure generally drifts upward in expectation (E[S_t|F_s] = S_s*e^(mu*(t-s)) for mu>0), because investors demand compensation for risk -- so it is not a martingale. The fundamental theorem of asset pricing says a market is arbitrage-free exactly when there exists a risk-neutral measure Q under which the discounted price e^(-rt)*S_t IS a martingale; under Q, the stock's drift is replaced by the risk-free rate r itself, and discounting by e^(-rt) exactly cancels that drift, leaving zero expected change. This is the entire mathematical foundation of risk-neutral option pricing: fair derivative prices are discounted expected payoffs under Q, precisely because that pricing rule is consistent with the no-arbitrage martingale condition.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd be precise about what's being claimed: a martingale isn't just 'no obvious trend,' it's the exact statement that your best forecast of the future value, given everything you know now, is the current value, full stop. A real-world stock price doesn't satisfy that -- it drifts up on average because investors demand compensation for risk, so E[S_t|F_s] grows at rate mu, not zero. What makes this all connect to arbitrage is the fundamental theorem of asset pricing: a market is arbitrage-free exactly when some risk-neutral measure Q exists under which the DISCOUNTED price is a martingale, and under Q the drift becomes r, so discounting by e^(-rt) removes it exactly. That equivalence is the whole reason 'discount the expected payoff under Q' is the correct way to price any derivative.
commonMistakes: Assuming any stock price process should be a martingale under the real-world measure
Forgetting discounting is what removes the risk-free drift to make the Q-measure price a martingale
Not connecting the martingale property directly to the formal statement of no-arbitrage
keyPoints: Martingale = zero expected drift conditional on the present
Raw real-world price drifts upward (mu>0), so it's not a martingale
Under the risk-neutral measure Q, drift becomes r, and discounting by e^(-rt) removes it, making the discounted price a martingale
This equivalence IS the fundamental theorem of asset pricing's no-arbitrage condition

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly states the martingale definition and why raw price fails it
Correctly explains the risk-neutral measure and discounting mechanism
Correctly connects this to the fundamental theorem of asset pricing / no-arbitrage

questions.title: Where the -0.5*sigma^2 Term in GBM's Solution Actually Comes From
questions.prompt: A junior analyst substitutes d(ln S) = dS/S = mu*dt + sigma*dW directly and gets E[ln(S_t)] - ln(S_0) = mu*t. The correct answer has an extra -0.5*sigma^2*t term. Using Ito's lemma, explain exactly where that correction comes from.
questions.modelAnswer: The naive substitution treats d(ln S) like an ordinary total differential, which is only valid in ordinary calculus. Stochastic calculus requires Ito's lemma: for f(S)=ln(S) under dS=mu*S*dt+sigma*S*dW, df = [df/dt + mu*S*(df/dS) + 0.5*sigma^2*S^2*(d^2f/dS^2)]dt + sigma*S*(df/dS)*dW. With df/dS=1/S and d^2f/dS^2=-1/S^2, the bracket becomes mu*S*(1/S) + 0.5*sigma^2*S^2*(-1/S^2) = mu - 0.5*sigma^2 -- the extra -0.5*sigma^2 term comes directly from the second-order Taylor term in Ito's lemma, which exists specifically because Brownian motion has nonzero quadratic variation, (dW)^2=dt, unlike an ordinary smooth function where that term would vanish. The naive substitution simply drops this term, which is exactly the bug.
questions.professionalAnswer: The analyst's mistake is applying the ordinary chain rule to a stochastic process, which just isn't valid -- Ito's lemma is the correct replacement, and it has one extra term beyond the ordinary chain rule: 0.5*sigma^2*(d^2f/dS^2)*dt. Plugging f(S)=ln(S) into that extra term specifically, with the second derivative -1/S^2 and the GBM diffusion coefficient sigma*S, gives exactly -0.5*sigma^2 after the S's cancel -- that's not an arbitrary correction factor, it's the direct output of the formula applied to this specific function. The deeper reason that extra term exists at all is (dW)^2=dt -- Brownian motion's quadratic variation is nonzero, which ordinary calculus implicitly assumes away and stochastic calculus can't.
commonMistakes: Applying the ordinary chain rule to a stochastic process instead of Ito's lemma
Forgetting that (dW)^2=dt is the single rule responsible for the extra term, not some unrelated correction factor
Mixing up which function (ln(S), not S itself) Ito's lemma is being applied to
keyPoints: Ordinary chain rule doesn't apply to stochastic processes because (dW)^2=dt, not 0
Ito's lemma adds a 0.5*sigma^2*(d^2f/dS^2) term versus the ordinary chain rule
Applying it to f(S)=ln(S) produces exactly the -0.5*sigma^2 drift correction
This is why GBM's exact solution differs from the naive substitution

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly states Ito's lemma and its extra term versus the ordinary chain rule
Correctly derives the -0.5*sigma^2 term by applying it to f(S)=ln(S)
Correctly identifies (dW)^2=dt as the root cause

questions.title: Why You'd Bootstrap a Sharpe Ratio Instead of Deriving Its Confidence Interval Analytically
questions.prompt: Explain why the bootstrap is a natural tool for building a confidence interval around a Sharpe ratio estimate, and why the ordinary (i.i.d.) bootstrap can be the wrong tool if the underlying returns are autocorrelated.
questions.modelAnswer: The Sharpe ratio is a ratio of two correlated random quantities (mean return and standard deviation of return), and deriving its exact sampling distribution analytically is genuinely hard, especially once returns aren't assumed normal. The bootstrap sidesteps this entirely: resample the observed returns with replacement many times, recompute the Sharpe ratio on each resample, and use the resulting distribution's standard deviation (bootstrap SE) or percentiles (percentile CI) directly, with no closed-form derivation needed. The ordinary bootstrap assumes the observations are i.i.d., so resampling with replacement correctly mimics drawing a fresh sample; real daily returns often show autocorrelation (volatility clustering, momentum, mean reversion), which plain resampling destroys by shuffling observations independently, understating the true uncertainty. The fix is a block bootstrap, which resamples contiguous blocks of consecutive observations to preserve short-range dependence.
questions.professionalAnswer: The Sharpe ratio is annoying analytically because it's a ratio of two things that are themselves random and correlated with each other, and getting an exact formula for how that ratio varies sample to sample -- especially once you stop assuming normal returns -- is genuinely hard. The bootstrap just skips the derivation: resample with replacement a few thousand times, recompute the Sharpe each time, and read the standard deviation or percentiles straight off that empirical distribution. The catch is that plain resampling assumes each observation is independent of the others, and real daily returns usually aren't -- they cluster in volatility, so shuffling them independently destroys real structure and can understate how uncertain the estimate actually is. A block bootstrap, resampling whole chunks of consecutive days instead of single points, is the fix that keeps that short-range dependence intact.

Treating a bootstrap confidence interval as automatically correct without checking the i.i.d. assumption
Not recognizing that a wide bootstrap CI around a Sharpe estimate is itself useful information, not a failure of the method

This works well for a statistic like the Sharpe ratio that has no simple sampling distribution
Plain bootstrap assumes i.i.d. data, which real autocorrelated returns violate
Block bootstrap fixes this by resampling contiguous blocks instead of individual points

Correctly explains the bootstrap mechanism (resample, recompute, read off distribution)

questions.title: Explaining to a PM Why Their Manager's 'Alpha' Might Just Be SMB Exposure
questions.prompt: A portfolio manager claims a fund manager generates genuine alpha because their returns beat the market consistently. How would you use the Fama-French three-factor model to test whether that's really alpha, or just exposure to the size and value factors?
questions.modelAnswer: Regress the manager's excess returns on the market excess return, SMB, and HML: R_i - Rf = alpha + beta_mkt*(Rm-Rf) + beta_smb*SMB + beta_hml*HML + eps. If the manager's returns are fully explained by tilting toward small-cap and/or value stocks (statistically significant beta_smb and/or beta_hml), the regression's intercept, alpha, will shrink toward zero and become statistically indistinguishable from zero once those exposures are accounted for -- meaning the 'outperformance' was really just riding well-documented size and value premiums, not genuine skill beyond factor exposure. Only if alpha remains large and statistically significant after controlling for all three factors is there real evidence the manager is adding value beyond what passive factor exposure would have delivered.
questions.professionalAnswer: The test is a direct regression: excess return against market, SMB, and HML, and then look specifically at what's left over -- the intercept, alpha. If most of this manager's apparent outperformance disappears once you've controlled for a size tilt and a value tilt (statistically significant betas on SMB/HML), that's strong evidence they were never generating alpha in the first place, just riding factor premiums that you could have gotten far more cheaply from an index fund. I'd also check the statistical significance of the resulting alpha, not just its sign -- a positive but noisy point estimate for alpha after the regression isn't the same as a defensible 'this manager adds real value' claim.

Treating a positive raw alpha from a simple CAPM regression as proof of skill, without checking whether a multi-factor model explains it away
Not checking the statistical significance of the estimated alpha, just its sign or magnitude

questions.title: Why Two Highly Correlated Stocks Might Still Be a Terrible Pairs Trade
questions.prompt: Two stocks have a 0.85 correlation in their daily returns. A junior researcher proposes a pairs trade based on this. Explain why high return correlation alone doesn't justify a pairs trade, and what test you'd actually run first.
questions.modelAnswer: Correlation measures whether two series' short-term moves tend to go together, but a pairs trade needs something stronger -- cointegration, meaning a particular linear combination of the two price LEVELS is stationary (mean-reverting), not just that their day-to-day returns move together. Two stocks can be highly correlated in returns while their price levels drift apart indefinitely with no tendency to revert, which would make a pairs trade betting on the spread reverting a losing proposition; conversely, lower return correlation can still coexist with genuine cointegration in levels. The correct first test is the Engle-Granger procedure: regress one price level on the other to estimate a hedge ratio, then run an Augmented Dickey-Fuller test on the regression's residuals (the spread) -- rejecting the unit-root null on the spread is evidence of cointegration, which is what the pairs trade actually depends on, not the return correlation the researcher started with.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd stop the researcher before they build anything and explain the distinction directly: correlation is about returns moving together day to day; cointegration is a much stronger claim about the price LEVELS having a stable long-run relationship, which is the thing a pairs trade actually needs, since you're betting on a spread reverting, not on two assets just bouncing around together. It's entirely possible for 0.85-correlated stocks to have price levels that wander apart forever with no mean to revert to. The correct first test is Engle-Granger: regress one level on the other to get a hedge ratio, then run an ADF test on the residual spread -- rejecting the unit-root null there is the actual evidence you need, not the correlation number that kicked off the idea.
commonMistakes: Treating high return correlation as sufficient justification for a pairs trade
Not testing the spread (price levels, not returns) for stationarity directly
Running a plain ADF test on the spread without the correct regression step first, or not knowing statsmodels' coint() wraps this with properly adjusted critical values

Cointegration requires a stationary linear combination of the two price levels
The Engle-Granger method regresses one level on the other, then ADF-tests the residual spread
A pairs trade needs cointegration in levels, not just correlated returns

questions.title: Tuning XGBoost for Low-Signal Financial Features Without Overfitting
questions.prompt: Write XGBoost code to fit a return-prediction model with early stopping on a held-out validation set, and explain which three hyperparameters matter most for keeping the model from fitting noise in low-signal financial data.
questions.code:
from xgboost import XGBRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X_tr, X_val, y_tr, y_val = train_test_split(X_train, y_train, test_size=0.2, shuffle=False)

model = XGBRegressor(
    n_estimators=1000,
    learning_rate=0.02,
    max_depth=3,
    subsample=0.7,
    colsample_bytree=0.7,
    reg_alpha=0.1,
    reg_lambda=1.0,
    early_stopping_rounds=50,
    eval_metric="rmse",
    random_state=0,
)
model.fit(X_tr, y_tr, eval_set=[(X_val, y_val)], verbose=False)
questions.modelAnswer: The three knobs that matter most, roughly in order: a small learning_rate (0.01-0.05) paired with early stopping so the number of boosting rounds is decided by validation performance rather than guessed; a shallow max_depth (2-4), since financial signal rarely needs deep feature interactions and deeper trees have far more room to fit noise; and subsample/colsample_bytree (0.6-0.8) to inject randomness per tree that fights overfitting, with reg_alpha/reg_lambda as a secondary lever on top of those three.
questions.professionalAnswer: The code is fairly mechanical once you know the knobs: small learning_rate, shallow max_depth, meaningful subsampling, and early_stopping_rounds so the validation set -- not a guess -- decides how many rounds to actually run. The ordering I'd give someone new to this: learning_rate and early stopping first, because that pairing controls how long the model gets to keep chasing whatever's left in the residuals; max_depth second, because financial features rarely have the kind of deep interactions that justify a deep tree; subsample/colsample_bytree third, as an extra layer of randomness that fights overfitting on top of the first two. reg_alpha/reg_lambda are real levers too, but they're secondary to getting those three right first.

If the top-ranked feature instead shows values scattered on both sides of zero with no visible relationship to its own level, that ranking is misleading -- high mean absolute SHAP value just means 'this feature moves predictions around a lot,' not 'this feature moves them in a sensible, consistent direction.' questions.title: Why One Backtest Path's Sharpe Ratio Isn't Enough Evidence
questions.prompt: Sketch the logic of Combinatorial Purged Cross-Validation (CPCV): with N=6 groups and k=2 held out at a time, how many distinct train/test combinations does this produce, and why does looking at the resulting distribution of Sharpe ratios tell you more than a single walk-forward backtest's Sharpe ratio?
questions.code:
from itertools import combinations
import numpy as np

def cpcv_splits(n_samples, n_groups=6, k_test_groups=2, embargo_frac=0.01, label_end=None):
    groups = np.array_split(np.arange(n_samples), n_groups)
    embargo = int(n_samples * embargo_frac)
    for test_group_ids in combinations(range(n_groups), k_test_groups):
        test_idx = np.concatenate([groups[g] for g in test_group_ids])
        test_start, test_stop = test_idx.min(), test_idx.max() + 1
        train_idx = np.array([
            i for i in range(n_samples)
            if i not in test_idx
            and not (label_end[i] >= test_start and i < test_stop)
            and not (test_stop <= i < test_stop + embargo)
        ])
        yield test_group_ids, train_idx, test_idx
questions.modelAnswer: With N=6 groups and k=2 held out at a time, the number of distinct combinations is C(6,2)=15 -- each combination holds out a different pair of groups as the test set (with purging/embargoing applied around each), trains on the rest, and produces its own out-of-sample Sharpe ratio. A single walk-forward backtest gives exactly one realized out-of-sample path, which could easily be an unusually lucky (or unlucky) draw given how short and noisy financial history is; looking at the distribution across all 15 (or more, if reassembled into full paths) combinations reveals whether the strategy's apparent edge is consistent across different slices of held-out data or whether it depends heavily on which specific slice happened to land in the test set. A strategy with a high average Sharpe but enormous variance across combinations is a strategy that got lucky on some slices, which a single backtest number would never reveal.
questions.professionalAnswer: The count is just C(6,2)=15 -- pick which 2 of the 6 groups get held out, every way, with purging and embargoing applied fresh around each specific held-out pair so none of the 15 individually leaks. The reason this matters more than a single walk-forward Sharpe: one backtest path is one draw from a huge space of 'ways history could have played out' given how short and noisy financial data really is, and it's entirely possible for a mediocre strategy to look great on the one path you happened to test. Looking at the spread across all 15 combinations tells you something a single number never could -- whether the edge holds up consistently, or whether it's riding on one or two lucky slices of history.
commonMistakes: Treating a single walk-forward Sharpe ratio as a reliable point estimate rather than one draw from many possible outcomes
Not applying purging/embargoing within each held-out combination, reintroducing the exact leakage CPCV is meant to prevent
Focusing only on the average Sharpe across combinations and ignoring the spread
keyPoints: C(N,k) combinations, each purged/embargoed independently
A single backtest path is one draw, possibly a lucky or unlucky one
CPCV produces a distribution of out-of-sample Sharpe ratios instead of one number
High variance across combinations signals fragility a single-path backtest would hide

import numpy as np

# label_end[i] = i + 5 for a 5-day-forward return label

def purge_before(before_idx, label_end, test_start):
    # keep only training rows whose label resolves BEFORE the test span starts
    return before_idx[label_end[before_idx] < test_start]

# Example: before = indices[indices < test_start]
# purged_before = purge_before(before, label_end, test_start)

TimeSeriesSplit alone only guarantees that training rows have an earlier raw timestamp than test rows -- it has no concept of a label window extending beyond its own observation's timestamp. A training row at day 97 with a label window of [97,102] sits 'before' a test span starting at day 100 by raw timestamp, but its label was computed using days 100-102, which are inside the test span -- TimeSeriesSplit would happily include that row in training, training the model on information from the days it's about to be tested on.

The reason TimeSeriesSplit alone misses this: it only ever checks raw row position against the test boundary, with zero awareness that a label can be built from a forward-looking window that extends past the row's own timestamp. A row at day 97 looks perfectly 'before' a test span starting at day 100 by position alone, but if that row's label depends on days 100-102, the model trained on it has effectively seen inside the test window -- and TimeSeriesSplit has no mechanism to know that, because it was never told what a label_end even is.

questions.title: Shrinking a Noisy Covariance Matrix with Ledoit-Wolf
questions.prompt: You have 80 assets but only 120 observations -- the sample covariance matrix is nearly singular. Write the sklearn code to apply Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage, and explain why a shrunk estimate that's further from the true covariance matrix in one sample can still be the better choice in practice.
questions.code:
from sklearn.covariance import LedoitWolf

# returns_matrix: (120, 80) array of asset returns
lw = LedoitWolf().fit(returns_matrix)
shrunk_cov = lw.covariance_
shrinkage_intensity = lw.shrinkage_
questions.modelAnswer: Ledoit-Wolf blends the sample covariance toward a scaled-identity target with a data-driven intensity delta, which is a deliberately biased estimator whenever delta>0 and the target isn't exactly right. The reason a shrunk estimate can still win in practice is the bias-variance tradeoff: the sample covariance is unbiased but has high variance (especially with few observations relative to the number of assets), and that extra variance is concentrated in exactly the small eigenvalues that blow up under matrix inversion; a small amount of bias from shrinking can buy a large reduction in that variance, lowering the total expected error and producing a far better-conditioned matrix (dramatically lower condition number) that behaves much better once you actually need to invert it for portfolio optimization.
questions.professionalAnswer: The fit itself is one line -- LedoitWolf().fit() -- and it hands you both the shrunk covariance matrix and the fitted shrinkage intensity it used. The 'further from truth but still better' question is the bias-variance tradeoff playing out exactly as advertised: the sample covariance is unbiased, but with 80 assets and only 120 observations it's extremely noisy, and that noise concentrates in the small eigenvalues -- precisely the ones that get blown up when you invert the matrix for optimization. A little deliberate bias from shrinking buys a large cut in that variance, and the resulting matrix is dramatically better-conditioned, which is what actually matters once you're using it inside a portfolio optimizer rather than just admiring it in isolation.

Not checking the condition number before and after shrinkage to confirm numerical stability actually improved

questions.title: Filtering a Time-Varying Hedge Ratio with a Kalman Filter
questions.prompt: Write the pykalman code to track a hedge ratio beta_t that drifts slowly over time, where y_t = beta_t*x_t + noise, and explain why the Kalman filter can track this drift more accurately than a rolling-window OLS re-estimate of beta.
questions.code:
from pykalman import KalmanFilter

# x_returns, y_returns: 1D arrays; q = process noise var, r = observation noise var
kf = KalmanFilter(
    transition_matrices=[[1.0]],
    observation_matrices=x_returns.reshape(-1, 1, 1),
    transition_covariance=[[q]],
    observation_covariance=[[r]],
    initial_state_mean=[0.0],
    initial_state_covariance=[[1.0]],
)
state_means, state_covs = kf.filter(y_returns.reshape(-1, 1))
questions.modelAnswer: A rolling-window OLS re-estimate treats every observation inside the window as equally informative and completely ignores everything outside it, so it reacts to drift with a lag roughly equal to the window length and throws away information just outside the window that could still help. The Kalman filter instead models beta explicitly as a latent state that evolves (here, as a random walk) and optimally weighs each new observation against the filter's current uncertainty: when a new observation is informative relative to that uncertainty, the estimate updates meaningfully; when it isn't, the filter barely moves -- producing a continuously updated estimate that tracks genuine drift more closely than a window-based re-estimate.
questions.professionalAnswer: The pykalman setup treats x_t as a time-varying observation matrix and beta_t as the latent state following a simple random walk. The reason this beats a rolling-window re-estimate: a rolling window gives every observation inside it equal weight and zero weight to everything outside it, so by construction it reacts to drift with a lag tied directly to the window length. The Kalman filter instead keeps a running estimate of its own uncertainty and updates proportionally -- a new data point that's informative relative to that uncertainty moves the estimate meaningfully, one that isn't barely moves it at all -- so it tracks a genuinely drifting beta with less lag than any fixed-window approach can manage.

questions.title: Solving a Least-Squares Regression via QR Instead of the Normal Equations
questions.prompt: Explain why solving a linear regression via QR decomposition is generally preferred over directly computing (X'X)^-1 X'y when X has even mild collinearity, and write the NumPy/SciPy code that does it.
questions.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import solve_triangular

Q, R = np.linalg.qr(X)
beta_hat = solve_triangular(R, Q.T @ y)

# equivalently, and more robust in practice:
# beta_hat, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)
questions.modelAnswer: Computing (X'X)^-1 X'y directly squares X's condition number inside X'X (since the condition number of X'X is roughly the square of X's own condition number), so any mild ill-conditioning in X -- collinear regressors, nearly redundant features -- gets dramatically amplified before you even invert anything, risking a numerically unstable or wildly inaccurate solution. QR decomposition avoids forming X'X at all: factor X=QR (Q orthogonal, R upper triangular), then beta_hat solves the much better-conditioned triangular system R*beta_hat = Q'y by simple back-substitution, which is both faster and numerically far more stable, especially as collinearity increases.
questions.professionalAnswer: The core numerical fact to know: forming X'X squares the condition number of whatever conditioning problem X already has, so even mild collinearity in X becomes a much worse conditioning problem by the time you're inverting X'X directly. QR sidesteps this entirely by never forming X'X -- you factor X into an orthogonal Q and an upper-triangular R, then solve a triangular system by back-substitution, which is numerically far more stable. In practice I'd usually just reach for np.linalg.lstsq, which handles this robustly (via an SVD-based approach internally) without needing to hand-roll the QR solve, but it's worth knowing what it's avoiding under the hood.

Forgetting that np.linalg.lstsq already handles this robustly without needing to hand-roll the QR solve

QR avoids forming X'X entirely, solving a better-conditioned triangular system instead
np.linalg.qr plus a triangular solve, or simply np.linalg.lstsq, are the practical tools
This matters more as regressors become more collinear

questions.title: A Sharpe Ratio of 2.1 from the Best of 200 Tried Strategies
questions.prompt: A colleague reports a Sharpe ratio of 2.1 from the best-performing variant out of 200 strategy configurations they tried. How would you use the Deflated Sharpe Ratio to evaluate whether this is believable, and what does a DSR near 0.5 tell you?
questions.modelAnswer: The expected maximum Sharpe ratio across 200 trials, even if every single one had zero true skill, rises above zero purely from the mechanics of taking a max over many random draws, and rises further with how dispersed the 200 trials' Sharpe ratios were from each other. Compute that expected-maximum benchmark (a function of the number of trials and their Sharpe ratio dispersion), then evaluate the Probabilistic Sharpe Ratio of the observed 2.1 against THAT benchmark instead of zero, also adjusting for the sample's skewness and kurtosis -- that combination is the Deflated Sharpe Ratio. A DSR near 0.5 (or below) means the observed 2.1 is almost exactly what you'd expect from pure luck across 200 attempts, given how much those attempts' Sharpe ratios varied -- strong evidence the headline number reflects multiple-testing luck, not genuine skill, even though a Sharpe of 2.1 'above zero' would look impressive in isolation.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk the colleague through why 2.1 alone isn't the right number to react to: with 200 trials, even if every single one had zero true skill, the BEST of them would land well above zero just from the mechanics of taking a maximum over that many draws, and how far above zero depends on how dispersed those 200 Sharpe ratios were. DSR builds exactly that inflated benchmark and asks whether 2.1 clears it, not whether it clears zero, while also correcting for the sample's skew and kurtosis. A DSR landing near 0.5 is the answer that should worry them -- it says 2.1 is basically what you'd expect from pure luck across 200 attempts, not evidence of a real edge.
