questions.title: A Strategy That Looked Great in Backtest and Decayed in Paper Trading
questions.prompt: A strategy posted a strong Sharpe ratio in backtest, then its paper-traded performance quietly decayed toward zero over the following months. Using the Probability of Backtest Overfitting (PBO) framework, explain how you'd have caught this red flag before risking real capital.
questions.modelAnswer: Backtest decay -- strong in-sample performance that erodes once the strategy meets genuinely new data -- is close to the single most reliable symptom of an overfit result, but by the time you observe it in live/paper trading, the cost (time, capital, opportunity) has already been paid. Combinatorially Symmetric Cross-Validation (the method behind PBO) could have flagged this earlier: split the backtest history into several subsamples, form every possible way to combine half into an in-sample set and the other half into an out-of-sample set, and for each combination pick the best in-sample configuration and check whether it ranks above or below the out-of-sample median. If that in-sample winner is a below-median out-of-sample performer in most combinations -- a high PBO -- it's a direct, pre-trade signal that the strategy's selection process is picking up overfitting noise, exactly the pattern that later showed up as live decay.
questions.professionalAnswer: The decay observed in paper trading is the expensive, after-the-fact version of a check that could have run before any capital was risked. PBO is built exactly for that: split the backtest history into subsamples, form every symmetric way of combining half into in-sample and half into out-of-sample, and for each combination see whether the configuration that won in-sample is actually above or below the out-of-sample median. If it's below median most of the time -- a high PBO -- that's telling you, before you ever trade it, that the selection process is picking up overfitting noise rather than a real edge. I'd pair that with the minimum-backtest-length heuristic too, since the number of configurations tried bears directly on how much history you'd need to trust any of this in the first place.

questions.title: A GARCH(1,1) Model That Misses the Asymmetric Vol Response
questions.prompt: A fitted GARCH(1,1) model systematically underpredicts volatility the day after a large negative return, but does fine after a same-sized positive return. What's the most likely cause, and which model would you switch to?
questions.modelAnswer: This is the classic signature of the leverage effect -- in equity markets, negative return shocks raise future volatility by more than same-sized positive shocks, and plain GARCH(1,1) cannot represent this at all because its variance equation depends only on eps_(t-1)^2, which is identical regardless of the shock's sign. Switch to GJR-GARCH, which adds an indicator term gamma*I_(t-1)*eps_(t-1)^2 (active only when the prior shock was negative) that directly captures the asymmetry with one extra parameter, or to EGARCH, which models log-variance with a separate sign-and-magnitude term (gamma*z_(t-1)) and has the added benefit of guaranteeing positive variance without constraining parameters. Either extension should materially reduce the systematic underprediction after negative shocks that plain GARCH(1,1) shows.
questions.professionalAnswer: This pattern is a textbook leverage-effect signature, and plain GARCH(1,1) is the wrong model for it on principle, not just in this one instance -- its variance update only ever sees eps_(t-1) squared, so a negative and positive shock of the same size are completely indistinguishable to it, even though real equity markets react more to the negative one. I'd move to GJR-GARCH, which bolts on a single indicator term that activates only for negative shocks, or EGARCH, which models log-variance directly with separate sign and magnitude effects and has the nice side benefit of guaranteeing positive variance with no parameter constraints needed. Either one should directly fix the systematic underprediction the question describes; I'd compare both by AIC/BIC on the actual data before picking.

questions.title: A Model That Performs Great in Backtest but Fails After a Regime Shift
questions.prompt: A strategy trained and validated entirely during a multi-year calm, low-volatility period suddenly underperforms badly once markets turn turbulent. Using the Markov-switching framework, explain what likely happened and how you'd diagnose it going forward.
questions.modelAnswer: The strategy was implicitly calibrated to one regime's statistical properties -- the calm regime's lower mean/volatility -- and had no mechanism to detect or adapt when the market's actual generating process switched to a different regime (higher volatility, possibly different mean) that the training window never saw. A single GARCH-style model can capture volatility that rises and falls continuously, but it can't represent an abrupt, discrete jump between qualitatively different states the way a Hamilton-style Markov-switching model can. Going forward, diagnose this by fitting a 2-or-3-regime Markov-switching model to the full history (calm and turbulent periods both included) and monitoring the smoothed regime probabilities in near-real-time; a sharp shift in the estimated probability of being in the 'turbulent' regime is a direct, early warning signal that the environment the strategy was built for has changed, well before performance visibly degrades.

This is specifically a discrete-regime-shift failure, not just a continuous volatility change a GARCH model would already handle -- the fix going forward is to fit a 2- or 3-state Markov-switching model to the full history, including turbulent periods, and then monitor the smoothed regime probability in near-real-time as an early-warning signal. A sharp move in the estimated probability of being in the 'turbulent' state is exactly the kind of thing that should trigger a review of the strategy before its live performance visibly degrades, not after.

questions.title: Two Assets with Moderate Correlation That Crashed Together Anyway
questions.prompt: A risk model built on a correlation matrix and normal assumptions estimated only a modest joint-crash probability for two assets with 0.5 correlation -- then they crashed together during a market stress event far more often than the model predicted. What's the most likely modeling gap, and how would a copula address it?
questions.modelAnswer: The gap is almost certainly tail dependence -- a Gaussian (correlation-matrix-and-normal) model assumes the joint distribution is fully described by linear correlation, which is only true for jointly elliptical distributions like the multivariate normal; real asset returns often show tail dependence, where extreme moves in one asset coincide with extreme moves in another far more often than a normal model with the same overall correlation would predict. A copula separates the dependence structure from each variable's own marginal distribution (Sklar's theorem); swapping the implicit Gaussian copula for a Student-t copula, built from a multivariate Student-t distribution, preserves the same linear correlation but produces meaningfully higher joint-tail probabilities, because the multivariate t distribution's shared random scaling factor can make everything move together violently at once -- exactly the pattern a correlation-and-normal risk model misses.
questions.professionalAnswer: The gap is tail dependence, and it's a gap specifically baked into assuming a Gaussian (correlation-and-normal) joint distribution -- that assumption says correlation fully describes dependence everywhere, including in the tails, which is only true for elliptical distributions like the multivariate normal. Real markets don't cooperate: two assets can look only moderately correlated most of the time and still crash together far more often than that correlation implies, because of tail dependence a Gaussian model structurally can't represent. A copula fixes this by separating the dependence structure from each asset's own marginal distribution; swapping in a Student-t copula at the exact same linear correlation produces meaningfully higher joint-tail probability, because the underlying multivariate-t construction lets everything move together violently at once in a way the Gaussian construction never allows.

Not checking whether the underlying risk model implicitly assumes a Gaussian copula (zero tail dependence) without stating that assumption explicitly
Treating the crash-together event as a one-off surprise rather than a predictable gap in the Gaussian-copula assumption

questions.title: A Model That Over-Weights One Volatility Event Dozens of Times
questions.prompt: Your triple-barrier labels use a 10-bar forward window, and a volatility spike on day 50 ends up influencing the label of every observation whose window covers that day. Explain why training a model naively on these labels effectively over-counts that one event, and how sample weighting fixes it.
questions.modelAnswer: Nearly every standard ML algorithm implicitly assumes each training row is an independent draw; with forward-looking labels like triple-barrier, that's false by construction -- a single event (the day-50 volatility spike) can influence the outcome of every label whose window covers that day, potentially dozens of labels in a row, so those labels are correlated with each other rather than independent. Treating them as independent means the model effectively sees that one event dozens of times, as if it happened repeatedly, inflating its apparent importance relative to genuinely unique events elsewhere in the history. The fix is to weight each label by its average uniqueness -- roughly 1 divided by the average concurrency (how many labels' windows cover a given bar) over its own window -- so a label that heavily overlaps many others gets down-weighted and doesn't dominate training the way independent observations would, passed directly via the sample_weight argument to .fit() in scikit-learn, XGBoost, or LightGBM.
questions.professionalAnswer: The over-counting happens because almost every ML algorithm assumes training rows are independent, and that assumption is simply false here by construction -- a single volatility event on day 50 shapes the outcome of every label whose 10-bar window touches that day, so dozens of 'different' training rows are really just the same underlying event dressed up as separate observations. Training naively on them means the model effectively sees that one event dozens of times over, as if it were dozens of independent occurrences, which distorts whatever it learns. The fix is average uniqueness: weight each label roughly by 1 over how much its window overlaps with others, so the day-50 cluster of labels gets collectively down-weighted and stops dominating the way truly independent observations would, fed in directly via sample_weight.
commonMistakes: Training with default (implicit equal) sample weights on overlapping labels without realizing the IID assumption is violated
Computing concurrency incorrectly (e.g. not accounting for each label's own window boundaries correctly)
Forgetting this same overlap problem also breaks naive cross-validation, not just training weights
keyPoints: Forward-looking labels overlap in time, breaking the IID assumption most ML algorithms rely on
Concurrency measures how many labels' windows cover a given point in time
Average uniqueness weights down heavily-overlapping labels
sample_weight in scikit-learn/XGBoost/LightGBM applies this directly during training

Correctly describes average uniqueness and how it fixes the over-counting

questions.title: A Fixed-Horizon Label That Calls a Stopped-Out Trade a Win
questions.prompt: Using fixed-horizon labeling, a position that blew through a painful stop-loss on day 2 but happened to recover by day 5 gets labeled a 'win.' Explain why this is a labeling design flaw, not a modeling flaw, and how the triple-barrier method fixes it.
questions.modelAnswer: Fixed-horizon labeling only looks at the return at a fixed number of bars ahead and ignores everything that happens in between -- it has no concept of a stop-loss or profit-take rule being triggered along the way. A position that hit a stop-loss on day 2 would, under any real trading discipline that actually enforces stop-losses, have been closed out at a loss right then; labeling it a 'win' because the price happened to recover by day 5 teaches the model a pattern no real trader following that discipline would ever have realized. The triple-barrier method fixes this by design: it labels each observation based on whichever of three barriers -- profit-take, stop-loss, or a maximum holding-period time barrier -- is touched FIRST, mirroring how a real position is actually managed, so the resulting label reflects an outcome a trading rule could genuinely have achieved rather than an artifact of checking only the endpoint.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is a labeling flaw, not something a better model could ever fix, because the label itself encodes a false premise -- that nothing which happened between day 0 and day 5 mattered except the final price. Any real position managed under an actual stop-loss discipline would have been closed out on day 2, at a loss, and never had the chance to 'recover' by day 5 at all; the fixed-horizon label is quietly assuming a trading rule nobody actually follows. The triple-barrier method is the direct fix: label based on whichever of profit-take, stop-loss, or the time barrier gets touched first, so the label reflects an outcome that a real, disciplined trading rule could actually have realized, not just a snapshot of where the price happened to land five days later.
commonMistakes: Assuming any model trained on fixed-horizon labels can be fixed with better features or more data, when the problem is in the labels themselves
Not realizing the triple-barrier method requires choosing profit-take/stop-loss/max-holding-period parameters that themselves need to reflect a realistic trading rule
Conflating triple-barrier labeling with meta-labeling, which is a separate, additional idea
keyPoints: Fixed-horizon labeling checks only the endpoint return, ignoring the path in between
This mislabels trades that would have been stopped out under any real risk discipline
Triple-barrier labels based on whichever of profit-take, stop-loss, or time barrier triggers first
The result reflects what a real trading rule could actually have realized, not just a snapshot at a fixed horizon

questions.title: Why a 20-Day LSTM Window Compounds the Leakage Problem from Chapter 4
questions.prompt: You're deciding whether to use an LSTM with a 20-day rolling input window for a daily return-prediction model. Explain why consecutive training examples here create a worse version of the overlapping-label leakage problem already covered for purged cross-validation, and how that should shape your validation design.
questions.modelAnswer: With a 20-day window stepped forward one day at a time, consecutive training examples overlap by 19 out of 20 days -- a far more severe version of the overlapping-outcome problem from sample weighting and purged cross-validation, except now it applies to every input WINDOW, not just the label's forward-looking horizon. This is easy to forget specifically because the leakage is baked into how the sequences were constructed in the first place, not just into how a train/test split was drawn afterward -- even a purged, leakage-free split on label windows can still leave training sequences whose INPUT windows heavily overlap test sequences' input windows. The validation design has to purge/embargo with the full extent of the input window in mind, not just the label horizon, and given the added overfitting risk from a large-parameter sequence model on low-signal financial data, this architecture should be reserved for settings with genuinely enough data (high-frequency microstructure) rather than used as a default upgrade over tree-based models.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd flag this before any code gets written: a 20-day sliding window stepped one day at a time means 19 out of every 20 days of INPUT are shared between consecutive training examples, which is a much bigger version of the overlapping-outcome problem already covered for labels. It's easy to miss because the leakage is baked into how the sequences are built, not into how the train/test split is later drawn -- you can purge perfectly on the label side and still have massive input-window overlap bleeding across the split. The validation design needs to purge/embargo based on the full input-window extent, not just the label horizon, and given how much bigger an LSTM's parameter count is relative to a tree model on the same low-signal data, I'd reserve this architecture for genuinely high-frequency settings with enough data to support it, not reach for it as a default upgrade.

Assuming a sequence model is a strict upgrade over tree-based models without weighing the added validation risk and parameter count
Not considering whether the data volume (daily vs. high-frequency) actually supports a large-parameter architecture at all

Leakage here is baked into sequence construction, not just the train/test split

questions.title: Designing a News-Sentiment Feature Pipeline Without Timing Leakage
questions.prompt: You're architecting a pipeline that scores news articles with a FinBERT-style model and turns the scores into a daily feature. What specific design choice prevents the text-specific version of look-ahead bias, and why is it easy to get wrong?
questions.modelAnswer: The feature must be timestamped by the article's actual PUBLICATION time, not by the fiscal period or event the article discusses -- an earnings report covering Q3 might be published in late October, and a feature built from it has to be attached to the October publication date, not backdated to the September 30 quarter-end it's reporting on. This is easy to get wrong because many data pipelines naturally index by the event or period a document is 'about,' since that's often the more analytically convenient join key, and it's a subtle, silent bug: the resulting backtest would hand the model sentiment information before it was actually publicly available, exactly the look-ahead bias problem seen elsewhere in this course, just manifesting through a text timestamp rather than a restated financial figure. The same caution applies to earnings-call transcripts, which aren't available until after the call ends, not at the start of the trading day the call happens to fall on.
questions.professionalAnswer: The design rule is simple to state and surprisingly easy to violate: timestamp every text-derived feature by when the article was actually PUBLISHED, never by the period or event it's describing. A Q3 earnings article published in late October has to carry an October timestamp in the pipeline, not a September 30 one, even though September 30 is the more natural join key against a fundamentals table. The reason this bug sneaks in is exactly that convenience -- pipelines are often built to join text and numeric data on the period they're both 'about,' and that join silently reintroduces look-ahead bias through the text side. The same discipline has to extend to transcripts specifically: a transcript isn't available until the call actually ends, not at market open on the day of the call.
commonMistakes: Timestamping a text-derived feature by the period/event it discusses rather than its actual publication/release time
Assuming this risk only applies to numeric fundamentals data and not to text
Not treating transcript availability (after the call ends) as its own timing constraint separate from the call's calendar date

questions.title: Vetting a New Satellite-Imagery Data Vendor Before It Reaches a Model
questions.prompt: A vendor offers a satellite-imagery feed estimating retail foot traffic, with 2.5 years of history. Outline the architecture/process you'd put in place before letting this feed anywhere near a production model, covering validation limits, data-quality review, and compliance.

questions.title: Why an RL Trading Agent That Looks Great in Simulation Might Fail Live
questions.prompt: A team trains a reinforcement-learning trading agent that performs excellently in its simulated market environment, then loses money consistently once deployed live. What's the most likely architectural gap in the simulation, and why is this a harder problem for RL than for the supervised models elsewhere in this course?
questions.modelAnswer: The most likely gap is that the simulated environment was too forgiving on market impact and transaction costs -- RL agents typically need enormous numbers of interactions to learn, far more than real market history can supply, so training largely happens in simulation, and if that simulation doesn't realistically model how the agent's OWN trades would move the price and what they'd cost, the agent learns a policy that exploits simulator artifacts rather than real, exploitable structure. This is a harder problem for RL specifically because the agent's actions are sequential and affect its own future state (unlike a static supervised prediction task), so simulation fidelity errors compound over an entire trajectory rather than showing up as a one-off prediction error, and the reward signal itself is delayed and noisy, making credit assignment (attributing a later P&L outcome to the specific actions that caused it) a genuinely harder problem on top of finance's already-low signal-to-noise ratio.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first suspect would be the simulator's market-impact and transaction-cost assumptions -- RL needs vastly more training interactions than real history can supply, so most of the learning happens in simulation, and if that simulation lets the agent trade size without moving the price or paying realistic costs, it will happily learn a policy that exploits exactly that unrealistic forgiveness. This is structurally harder for RL than for a supervised model here because the agent's actions are sequential and feed back into its own future state, so a simulation fidelity gap compounds across an entire trajectory rather than showing up as one bad prediction; on top of that, the reward is delayed and noisy, so even identifying which past actions deserve credit for a later P&L outcome is its own hard problem layered on top of finance's usual low signal-to-noise ratio.
commonMistakes: Training and validating an RL agent purely in simulation without a rigorous audit of the simulator's market-impact and cost assumptions
Treating RL as a drop-in upgrade over supervised approaches without accounting for its much larger data appetite
Underestimating the credit-assignment problem specific to delayed, sequential rewards

questions.title: Choosing DuckDB and Parquet Over a Row-Oriented Database for a Research Pipeline
questions.prompt: You're architecting storage for a research team that mostly runs queries like 'average return by sector across ten million rows.' Explain why columnar storage (Parquet/DuckDB) is architecturally the right choice here, and what would change your answer.
questions.modelAnswer: A columnar store keeps all values of one column together on disk, so a query like 'average the close column across ten million rows, grouped by sector' reads only the bytes it actually needs (close and sector), skipping every other column entirely -- exactly the shape of nearly every research (OLAP) query this team runs. A row-oriented database, by contrast, is built for the opposite pattern -- 'fetch this one record and all its fields' (OLTP) -- and would read irrelevant columns along with the ones that matter for an aggregation query. Columnar storage also compresses better (similar values stored contiguously) and supports vectorized execution (one operation across a whole column chunk at once), both of which showed roughly a 20x speedup over a naive Python filter-loop in a real benchmark. This answer would change if the workload shifted to genuinely high-frequency, continuously-arriving tick data needing sub-second live query latency -- at that point a purpose-built time-series database (or kdb+) earns its higher setup cost, not because the data is 'time-series' but because of the ingestion/latency requirement specifically.
questions.professionalAnswer: Columnar is the right call here because it matches the actual query shape: 'average a column across millions of rows, grouped by something' reads only the columns it needs and skips the rest, while a row-oriented database built for 'fetch one record with all its fields' would drag along irrelevant columns for the exact same query. On top of that, columnar storage compresses better and supports vectorized execution, and a real benchmark showed roughly a 20x speedup over a naive row-by-row Python approach on this kind of workload. What would change my answer is the workload shape, not the data size -- if this team suddenly needed sub-second queries against continuously-arriving tick data rather than end-of-day batch analysis, that's when a purpose-built time-series database earns its cost, specifically because of the latency and ingestion requirement, not because the data happens to be time-series.

Assuming 'large data' alone justifies specialized infrastructure when DuckDB/Parquet handle large batch workloads just fine

Row-oriented (OLTP) storage is built for a different access pattern research rarely needs
Compression and vectorized execution both contribute to columnar's real speed advantage
The case for specialized time-series infrastructure is ingestion/latency requirements, not data size or 'time-series-ness' alone

questions.title: Designing a Cache Key That Won't Silently Return a Stale Answer
questions.prompt: You're adding disk-based caching to an expensive backtest function with signature `run_backtest(signal_name, lookback, universe)`. What determines whether your cache key design is safe, and what's the specific failure mode if you get it wrong?
questions.modelAnswer: The cache key must include every argument that actually determines the output -- here, (signal_name, lookback, universe) -- no more and no less. Get it wrong in the 'too loose' direction (e.g., keying only on signal_name while lookback silently varies) and two genuinely different calls collide on the same cache entry, so the second call wrongly receives the first call's stale answer -- a silent, dangerous failure mode because nothing errors, the pipeline just returns a plausible-looking wrong number. Get it wrong in the 'too specific' direction (including an irrelevant argument, like a timestamp that changes every call) and the cache never hits twice, silently providing zero benefit while still looking like it's 'working.' The fix is disciplined, not clever: audit every argument that affects the result and include exactly those in the key, using something like diskcache so the cache survives process restarts.
questions.professionalAnswer: The whole safety question comes down to one audit: does the key include every argument that actually determines the output, exactly those and no others? Get it too loose -- say, keying only on signal_name while lookback quietly varies between calls -- and you get the dangerous failure mode: two genuinely different calls collide on the same key, and the second one silently receives the first one's stale, wrong answer, with no error anywhere to flag it. Get it too specific -- including something irrelevant like a timestamp -- and the cache just never hits, which wastes the effort of adding it but at least isn't dangerous. I'd use diskcache specifically so this survives process restarts, and I'd test explicitly that a genuinely different lookback produces a cache miss, not just that a repeated call produces a hit.
commonMistakes: Keying the cache on a subset of the arguments that actually determine the output, risking stale-answer collisions
Including irrelevant arguments in the key, silently defeating the cache's purpose
Not testing that a genuinely different call (e.g. a different lookback) correctly misses the cache rather than assuming it does

Too loose a key causes silent stale-answer collisions, the dangerous failure mode
Too specific a key causes silent cache misses that defeat the cache's purpose without erroring

questions.title: When a Quant Team Actually Needs kdb+ Instead of DuckDB
questions.prompt: A trading desk asks whether they should migrate their research data infrastructure from DuckDB/Parquet to kdb+. What questions would you ask to determine whether that migration is actually justified?
questions.modelAnswer: The determining factor is ingestion and latency requirements, not data size or 'it's time-series data' alone -- ask whether the workload involves genuinely high-frequency, continuously-arriving tick data (not end-of-day or minute bars), whether live queries need to run against data that's still being written with sub-millisecond-to-low-millisecond latency requirements, and whether the infrastructure needs to serve that data to other systems (a real-time risk or market-making system) rather than just supporting one research team's batch analysis. questions.title: Deciding Whether a Backtesting Engine Needs a Class Hierarchy
questions.prompt: You're designing a backtesting engine that needs to track positions as fills arrive and support multiple interchangeable trading strategies. Explain why this is a case where object-oriented design genuinely earns its place, and what you'd use composition for versus inheritance.
questions.modelAnswer: This is exactly the case where a class helps: there's real state that persists and changes over time (positions changing as fills arrive) with behavior tied to that state ('what's my current exposure' needs the current state, not a fresh recomputation), which is the test for when OOP is worth the structure. A PositionBook (a @dataclass-based class tracking a dict of positions, with an add_fill method) is a natural fit, and a Strategy base class with a generate_signal(data) -> Signal method that each concrete strategy overrides captures the genuine 'is-a' relationship where inheritance is appropriate -- different strategies really are variations on a shared interface. But the PositionBook itself should use COMPOSITION for anything else it needs, like a RiskLimits object it holds and calls methods on, rather than inheriting from it -- there's no 'is-a' relationship there, just a 'has-a' one, and composition keeps the pieces swappable and the hierarchy from becoming rigid.
questions.professionalAnswer: This passes the test for when a class is actually worth it: there's genuine persisting state (positions, updated as fills arrive) with real behavior attached to that state ('what's my current exposure' needs to read the current state, not recompute from nothing). A PositionBook built with @dataclass and an add_fill method is the natural home for that. For the strategies, a Strategy base class with a generate_signal method that each concrete strategy overrides is a legitimate inheritance case -- there's a real is-a relationship, since every concrete strategy genuinely is a variation on the same interface. Everything else, like a RiskLimits object the PositionBook needs to consult, I'd handle with composition instead -- it's a has-a relationship, not an is-a one, and composition keeps those pieces swappable without locking the design into a rigid hierarchy.

questions.title: Being Interrupted Mid-Presentation with a Challenging Question
questions.prompt: You're three minutes into presenting your capstone research in an onsite interview loop when a senior researcher interrupts with a pointed, skeptical question you hadn't fully anticipated. How do you handle the interruption without losing control of the room?
questions.modelAnswer: Treat the interruption as exactly what it is -- the skeptical-audience exercise arriving early, not a derailment -- rather than reacting defensively or trying to redirect back to your prepared script. Repeat the question back in one sentence to confirm you understood it correctly and to buy yourself a moment to think, then answer the actual question asked directly before adding any additional context, rather than pivoting immediately to a prepared talking point that doesn't quite address what was asked. If you genuinely don't know the answer, say so plainly and name what you'd need to check or compute to find out -- a confident, specific 'I don't know, here's how I'd verify that' lands far better with a quant interviewer than a guess that turns out wrong, since it demonstrates exactly the intellectual honesty the whole interview process is designed to test for.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd treat this exactly as the skeptical-audience moment the whole capstone defense was built to prepare me for, not a derailment of my planned talk. I'd repeat the question back in one sentence -- partly to confirm I heard it right, partly to buy myself a second to actually think -- and then answer the real question asked before I add any of the context I'd planned to lead with. If I genuinely don't have the answer, I'd say so directly and name exactly what I'd check to find out, because a specific 'I don't know, here's how I'd verify it' reads far better to a quant interviewer than a confident guess that turns out wrong.

questions.title: Comparing a Systematic Fund Offer Against a Prop Shop Offer
questions.prompt: You have two offers with the same headline base salary -- one from a systematic hedge fund with a team-performance bonus, one from a prop shop with an individual-PnL-tied profit share. How do you evaluate which is actually the better offer, beyond the matching base number?
questions.modelAnswer: Recognize first that a matching base salary tells you almost nothing about expected total compensation or its variance, because the two bonus structures behave completely differently: a team-performance bonus at the systematic fund ties your pay to the fund or team's overall results, smoothing out individual variance but also meaning your pay depends on others' work; an individual-PnL-tied profit share at the prop shop can pay far more in a good personal year and far less in a bad one, concentrating both the upside and the risk on your own performance. Build a researched range for each structure specifically (not a generic 'quant salary' number), and then weigh the decision beyond compensation entirely: which firm's risk culture and research rigor actually matches the honest-cost-modeling, real-out-of-sample-validation standard you were trained to value, which offers better mentorship and learning, and what's your own genuine tolerance for profit-share-style variance versus a steadier structure.
questions.professionalAnswer: The matching base number is basically a distraction here -- the two bonus structures imply very different expected total compensation and very different variance. A team-performance bonus smooths things out but ties my pay partly to other people's results; an individual-PnL profit share concentrates both the upside and the downside risk on my own performance specifically, which can mean a great year pays far more and a bad year pays far less than the steadier structure. I'd research a specific range for each structure rather than treating 'quant comp' as one number, and then weigh the decision beyond pay entirely -- which firm's actual research culture matches the honest, rigorous standard I was trained to hold myself to, which offers better mentorship, and how much profit-share-style variance I can genuinely tolerate.
commonMistakes: Comparing only the headline base salary, treating it as representative of total expected compensation
Not researching typical bonus/profit-share ranges separately for each specific firm type
Deciding purely on compensation structure without weighing risk culture, mentorship, and day-to-day role fit
keyPoints: Matching base salaries can hide very different total-compensation structures and variance
Team-performance bonuses and individual-PnL profit shares carry different risk/reward tradeoffs
Build a researched compensation range specific to each firm type, not one generic number
Weigh risk culture, mentorship, and genuine tolerance for pay variance alongside the number itself

questions.title: Being Handed an Ambiguous Research Brief by a New PM
questions.prompt: A new PM hands you a one-line brief: 'see if there's a reversal effect in sector ETFs.' Based on how a real capstone brief should be scoped, what would you push back on or clarify before writing any code?
questions.modelAnswer: Push back gently to turn the vague mandate into something specific and falsifiable before touching any data: what exact universe (which sectors, over what date range, accounting for ETFs that didn't exist for the whole period, like a real point-in-time universe would require), what horizon defines 'reversal' (5-day, 10-day, something else), and what would actually count as a meaningful, tradable effect versus a statistical curiosity (a specific significance threshold, a net-of-cost Sharpe ratio target, survival through specific historical stress windows). Getting these specifics agreed with the PM up front, before any result exists, is exactly the preregistration discipline that prevents the research from quietly becoming 'try reversal at five different horizons until one looks significant' -- a one-line brief is a starting point for a conversation, not something to start coding against literally.
questions.professionalAnswer: A one-line brief like that is a conversation starter, not a spec I'd start coding against directly. I'd ask for the specifics that actually determine the research design: which sectors, over what date range, and critically, how we handle ETFs that didn't exist for the whole sample (a real point-in-time universe issue, not an edge case to brush past); what horizon actually defines 'reversal' -- 5-day, 10-day, something else; and what would count as a real, worth-trading effect versus a statistical curiosity, agreed before any result exists. Getting that agreement up front is exactly the preregistration discipline that keeps an open-ended mandate from quietly turning into 'try five horizons until one looks significant.'

Silently picking a convenient universe/date range without checking it against what's actually point-in-time correct
Not agreeing on success criteria with the PM before any results exist, inviting goalpost-moving later

Clarify universe, horizon, and success criteria with the stakeholder up front
Respect point-in-time universe constraints (e.g. ETFs that launched partway through the sample)
This preregistration discipline prevents an open-ended mandate from becoming an unconscious multiple-testing exercise

questions.title: Reporting a Statistically Significant but Modest Reversal Effect Honestly
questions.prompt: Your analysis finds a small but statistically significant reversal effect (correlation around -0.07, HAC-corrected t-stat around -2.4), concentrated in high-volatility regimes. How do you present this finding to a team expecting a more dramatic result, without overselling or underselling it?
questions.modelAnswer: Present the number exactly as it is -- small, statistically significant after correcting for overlapping-window autocorrelation with Newey-West standard errors, and NOT overwhelming -- rather than either inflating its importance to meet expectations or downplaying it out of disappointment that it isn't bigger. The genuinely interesting and more persuasive part of the finding is the regime-dependence: the effect is significant and stronger in high-volatility periods and statistically indistinguishable from zero in calm periods, which is a more convincing pattern than an isolated significant number because it's consistent with an economic story (overreaction during fear, not during calm) rather than an unexplained statistical artifact. Disclose the honest caveats too -- that several related cuts of the same dataset were tested (a data-snooping risk) and that overlapping windows mean the effective sample size is smaller than the raw day-count suggests -- rather than letting the team walk away more confident than the evidence actually supports.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd report the exact number, exactly as significant as it actually is -- small, real after the Newey-West correction, but genuinely modest, not the dramatic headline the team might be hoping for. What I'd actually lead with, though, is the regime-dependence, because it's the more persuasive part of the story: the effect holds up in high-volatility periods and essentially disappears in calm ones, which fits a real economic mechanism (overreaction during fear) rather than being an unexplained number that just happened to clear a significance threshold. And I'd disclose the honest caveats alongside it -- several related cuts of the same data were tested, and overlapping windows mean the effective sample size is smaller than the raw day-count implies -- rather than let the team walk away more confident in this than the evidence actually supports.
commonMistakes: Inflating a modest, honestly-qualified result to meet a team's expectations for a dramatic finding
Downplaying a genuinely interesting regime-dependent pattern just because the headline correlation number looks small in isolation
Omitting the data-snooping and small-effective-sample-size caveats because they complicate an otherwise clean-sounding result
keyPoints: Report the exact magnitude and significance level honestly, neither inflated nor downplayed
The regime-dependence pattern (significant in high-vol, absent in low-vol) is more persuasive than an isolated correlation number
Disclose data-snooping risk from testing multiple related cuts of the same dataset
Disclose that overlapping windows reduce the effective sample size below the raw day-count

Leads with the regime-dependence as the more persuasive finding
Discloses data-snooping and effective-sample-size caveats

questions.title: Mentoring a Junior Researcher Whose First Backtest Just Failed
questions.prompt: A junior researcher you're mentoring just got a disappointing, close-to-zero Sharpe ratio on their first independent backtest and seems discouraged. How do you handle this mentoring moment?
questions.modelAnswer: Reframe the result immediately and genuinely, not as a consolation: a carefully-run backtest that honestly reports a near-zero Sharpe ratio is a successful piece of research, not a failed one -- it tested a real hypothesis properly and found nothing, which is useful, documentable information, and is a far better outcome than a backtest with a hidden leak that reports an impressive but fake number. Walk through the result together to confirm it's a genuine null and not a bug (checking the usual culprits -- look-ahead bias, survivorship bias, cost modeling), and if it holds up, help them write it up properly as a documented negative finding rather than quietly shelving it, so the next person doesn't waste a week rediscovering the same dead end. The mentoring goal is to model that intellectual honesty about a disappointing result is the actual skill being developed here, not a stepping stone to be embarrassed about.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd reframe this immediately, and genuinely mean it: a carefully-run backtest that honestly comes back near zero is successful research, not a failed project -- it's a real hypothesis tested properly, with nothing hidden or forced. Before discussing what it means, though, I'd walk through it with them to confirm it's a genuine null and not a bug -- the usual look-ahead bias, survivorship bias, cost-modeling checks -- because that verification step matters regardless of how the result feels. If it holds up as a real null, I'd help them write it up properly rather than let it quietly disappear, so the next person on the team doesn't spend a week rediscovering the same dead end. The real point of this mentoring moment is showing them that being honest about a disappointing result is the actual skill, not something to be embarrassed about.
commonMistakes: Letting the junior researcher internalize a null result as a personal failure rather than a normal, useful research outcome
Skipping the verification step (confirming it's a genuine null, not a bug) before discussing what it means
Not helping them document the finding, leaving the lesson learned only in their own head
keyPoints: A well-run backtest that honestly reports a null result is successful research, not a failure
Verify the null isn't actually a pipeline bug before discussing its meaning
Help the junior researcher document the finding so others don't repeat the same dead end
Model that intellectual honesty about disappointing results is the real skill being taught

questions.title: Disagreeing with a Senior Quant's Modeling Choice
questions.prompt: A senior researcher on your team wants to use a plain K-fold cross-validation on a time-series return-prediction model, which you know leaks future information into training. How do you raise this disagreement respectfully, given the seniority difference?
questions.modelAnswer: Raise it as a specific technical concern grounded in a concrete mechanism, not a vague objection to their judgment: explain exactly how plain K-fold rotates which fold is held out, so for every fold except the first, training data includes rows from after the test period in calendar time, inflating validation scores. Bring the concrete fix (TimeSeriesSplit, or purged/embargoed cross-validation if labels overlap) rather than just the critique, and frame it as a shared goal -- getting a validation number the team can actually trust -- rather than a challenge to their competence. If they still prefer their approach after hearing the technical argument, ask to see a quick side-by-side comparison of both validation schemes' results, which usually settles the disagreement with evidence rather than continued argument, and preserves the relationship either way.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd ground this in the specific mechanism rather than a vague 'I don't think that's right' -- plain K-fold rotates which fold gets held out, so for every fold except the first, the training set includes rows from after the test period in calendar time, which inflates the validation score in a way that's easy to miss if you're not looking for it specifically. I'd bring the fix along with the concern, not just the critique -- TimeSeriesSplit, or purged/embargoed CV if the labels overlap -- and frame the whole thing around a shared goal, getting a number the team can actually trust, rather than anything about their competence. If they still want to go with their original approach after that, I'd suggest running both side by side and comparing -- that usually settles it with evidence rather than continued back-and-forth, and it doesn't put either of us in a position of just asserting we're right.
commonMistakes: Raising the disagreement vaguely ('I don't think that's right') instead of with the specific mechanism and a concrete fix
Treating the seniority gap as a reason to stay silent about a real technical leakage risk
Making the disagreement personal or about competence rather than about the specific validation choice
keyPoints: Ground a technical disagreement in the specific mechanism, not a vague objection
Bring a concrete alternative (TimeSeriesSplit or purged CV), not just a critique
Frame the disagreement around a shared goal (trustworthy validation), not a challenge to seniority or competence
Offering to run a side-by-side comparison often resolves the disagreement with evidence

Proposes bringing a concrete fix, not just the critique
Frames the disagreement respectfully around a shared goal
